L	“Solitude and leadership—what can they possibly have to do with each other?” The question appears
paradoxical. Leadership is commonly imagined as a public performance: a figure at the head of an
army, a corporation, or a nation. Solitude, by contrast, evokes withdrawal—a man alone in the woods,
cut off from collective life. The essay challenges this contrast and argues that solitude is not the enemy
of leadership but its necessary precondition. Modern systems of education and _ professional
advancement, the author contends, prioritise success over judgment. Elite institutions excel at
producing individuals who can accumulate credentials, satisfy expectations, and follow established
paths. Such people are efficient and articulate, yet fundamentally unreflective. They can answer
questions posed by others but lack the capacity to frame their own. Achievement, divorced from
independent thought, results in authority without vision. Bureaucracy amplifies this failure. Drawing
on literary archetypes, the essay depicts bureaucratic leaders as ordinary, interchangeable figures who
maintain routines rather than originate ideas. Hierarchies reward compliance, manoeuvring, and
silence. Advancement depends less on moral courage than on the ability to “get along by going along,”
until leadership becomes an empty role rather than an act of judgment.
Solitude is presented as the corrective. Genuine thinking requires distance from constant stimulation
and noise. The modern celebration of multitasking is dismissed as a myth that undermines depth and
clarity. First thoughts, the author observes, are usually borrowed; solitude allows individuals to move
beyond convention and encounter their own reasoning. Solitude need not mean isolation. It can take
the form of deep reading, sustained focus, introspection, or long, uninterrupted conversation.
Ultimately, leadership is described as an intensely solitary responsibility. When rules fail and
authority offers no guidance, the leader stands alone—with nothing but judgment shaped in solitude.
Source: William Deresiewicz, “Solitude and Leadership,” The American Scholar, March 1, 2010 (lecture
delivered at the United States Military Academy, West Point, October 2009).

II.	Nancy’s trouble begins with a mistake so small it feels harmless: confusing one weekday for another.
She dismisses it as memory, not mind, expecting reassurance from her doctor. Instead, she finds herself
referred to a specialist who treats elderly patients, a development that unsettles her far more than the
error itself. What disturbs Nancy is not illness but the suspicion that something inside her is quietly
loosening.
Determined to retain control, she decides to locate the doctor’s office the evening before her
appointment. The choice reveals her fear of appearing confused or dependent. As she walks through the
town of Highman, the surroundings echo her inner unease. Shuttered shops, broken clocks, empty
streets, and misleading signs suggest a world that no longer operates by reliable markers. Nancy
recalls details vividly but forgets essentials—names, directions, and purposes. A scrap of paper meant
to guide her turns out to be meaningless.
Her wandering brings her to an unexpectedly beautiful garden, alive with flowers and fountains. Its
owner, a reserved man dressed in black, speaks to her with calm detachment. Their conversation feels
soothing, grounded in fragments of the past. When Nancy asks whether there once were “more sensible
explanations” for things, the question carries a personal weight rather than philosophical curiosity.
Acting on the man’s suggestion, Nancy drives to a rest home outside town. The building appears warm
and welcoming, but once inside, panic takes hold. Doors do not open. No one responds. Isolation presses
in, and fear overwhelms her.
The truth arrives quietly. A nurse addresses Nancy with familiarity. She is not visiting the home—she
belongs there. The journey through town was not a search for a doctor, but a return to memory. When
Nancy recalls her husband and her former independence, it becomes clear that what she has lost is not
direction, but time itself.
Source: Adapted from a literary short story exploring memory loss, ageing, and dementia

Til.	A night-time walk begins with irritation rather than reflection. Darkness feels hostile: the road is
uneven, streetlights are missing, and visibility is limited. The immediate response is to regard the dark
as unsafe and unnecessary, something modern life has worked to overcome. Light, by contrast, is
associated with order, progress, and control. Darkness appears to belong to an earlier stage of
development.
This perception does not remain unchanged. As the walk continues, the idea of an International Dark
Sky Park emerges—an area where artificial illumination is deliberately restricted. In such spaces, the
night sky is no longer obscured by human lighting. The Milky Way becomes clearly visible, sometimes
resembling early dawn. Darkness, once treated as absence, begins to register as presence.
Gradually, darkness is recast as preservation rather than deprivation. It allows room for wonder,
imagination, and perspective. Constant illumination, it is suggested, has reduced human sensitivity to
scale and mystery. When everything is visible, little feels significant; when nothing is concealed, depth
disappears. Darkness restores proportion by reminding humans of their limited place within a vast
universe.
The discussion extends beyond astronomy into ethical and psychological concerns. Darkness comes to
represent restraint—the decision not to dominate every environment or eliminate every uncertainty.
Just as natural systems depend on cycles of night to function, the human mind requires periods of
obscurity to reflect, imagine, and recalibrate.
Technology is not rejected, nor is a return to the past encouraged. Instead, balance is emphasised.
Protecting darkness is framed not as opposition to progress, but as a way of preserving a fragile human
capacity: the ability to experience awe without possession and beauty without explanation. Stepping
away from constant light is presented not as loss, but as an opportunity to recover perspective,
humility, and connection.
Source: Adapted from “Let There Be Dark” by Regan Penaluna, Nautilus, February 3, 2026.

IV.	Byrnihat, an industrial town located on the Assam—Meghalaya border, has emerged as an example of
the environmental costs associated with rapid economic expansion. According to the IQAir World Air
Quality Report for 2024, published in March 2025, Byrnihat was ranked as the world’s most polluted
metropolitan area. The report recorded an annual average PM2.5 concentration of 128.2 micrograms
per cubic metre, a level significantly higher than the World Health Organization’s guideline of 5
micrograms per cubic metre.
Industrial activity is identified as the primary contributor to this condition. The town hosts around 80
operational factories, including cement plants, steel units, and distilleries. Industrial expansion has
proceeded at a rapid pace, with limited regulatory oversight. Byrnihat’s geographical location further
intensifies the problem. Situated in a valley surrounded by hills, the town experiences poor dispersion
of pollutants, causing emissions to accumulate rather than dissipate.
Daily life in the town unfolds alongside this industrial presence. Residential areas and recreational
spaces exist close to factory zones. Smoke from industrial units often reduces visibility, particularly in
the evenings. Pollution has become a constant feature rather than an occasional occurrence.
Health impacts have been increasingly reported. Medical practitioners and residents note a rise in
respiratory illnesses such as asthma and tuberculosis, along with an increase in cancer cases. These
conditions are linked to prolonged exposure to polluted air. Regulatory mechanisms appear ineffective.
Anti-pollution norms are frequently violated, and pollution control equipment in several factories is
reported to be non-functional. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Workers in cement factories face heightened risk due to regular inhalation of silica dust. Prolonged
exposure has led to cases of silicosis, a condition that often progresses into tuberculosis. Concerns have
also been raised about institutional oversight. Observers note that industrial permissions are granted
with limited assessment, and regulatory bodies lack autonomy. The situation reflects broader questions
about governance, regulation, and the balance between economic growth and public health.
Source: Anurab Dhar, “Poisoned by growth,” Frontline (The Hindu Group), Digital Exclusive photo

V.	In the hospital ward, Leonard Thompson barely spoke. At fourteen, he had learned that effort was
expensive. When nurses asked how he felt, he answered with a shrug, conserving breath. His father
once tried optimism.
“Just a little longer,” he said. Leonard looked past him. He had heard that sentence before. The doctors
spoke quietly near the bed. “There isn’t much more we can do,” one of them said, not unkindly.
Diabetes, at the time, did not invite debate. It closed conversations. Then a different voice entered the
room. “We’d like to try something new,” Frederick Banting explained to Leonard’s parents. “It may not
work.”
Florence Thompson asked the only question that mattered. “And if we don’t try?”
Banting didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. The first injection did nothing. Leonard noticed the silence
that followed, heavier than before. No one said the word failure, but it hung in the air. He turned his
face to the wall. The familiar attitude returned: endure, expect nothing. Days later, another injection.
Then another. A nurse leaned closer and smiled. “You're brighter today,” she said.
Leonard frowned. “I feel... less tired,” he admitted, surprised by his own voice.
The change was slow but undeniable. “He asked for food,” a doctor noted, almost incredulous. “He sat
up.” Leonard himself tested the improvement cautiously, as if it might vanish if acknowledged too
quickly. When his father said, “You’re getting stronger,” Leonard replied, “Maybe,” but this time he
didn’t look away.
Elsewhere, confidence was hardening into belief. Banting, exhausted but alert, told a colleague, “It
works—but it has to work for everyone.” When asked about patents, he dismissed the idea. “Insulin
doesn’t belong to us. It belongs to the world.”

the Enforcement Directorate (ED) can file writ petitions before High Courts under Article 226 of the
Constitution to enforce its rights as a juristic person. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs
for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for other purposes, traditionally allowing individuals
and entities affected by state action to seek judicial remedies. The controversy arose after the Kerala
High Court upheld the ED’s right to approach it under Article 226, treating the ED as a juristic entity
entitled to file such petitions, meaning a non-human legal entity which, like a natural person, can
enforce certain rights in court.
A Division Bench of the Supreme Court, comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra
Sharma, issued notices on the appeals filed by the Kerala and Tamil Nadu governments challenging
this High Court ruling. These state governments argue that the ED an investigative agency constituted
under statutory law — does not qualify as a juristic person with standing to invoke Article 226. In
Kerala’s petition before the apex court, it was contended that only entities explicitly conferred with the
power to sue by statute should be recognised as juristic persons, and that the ED does not fall under
this category. Tamil Nadu has filed a similar appeal, asserting that the Kerala High Court’s reasoning
has encouraged the ED to pursue writ petitions in other High Courts, including Madras, in cases where
the agency seeks to quash criminal proceedings instituted by the State.
The Kerala High Court’s original order, dated 26 September 2025, came in the backdrop of a judicial
inquiry into alleged overreach by central agencies, including the ED and Customs, in a gold smuggling
case involving political leaders. The High Court upheld an interim stay order that restrained the
judicial probe into the ED’s investigation, finding merit in the ED’s petition and effectively accepting

not ordinarily recognised as juristic persons can directly approach High Courts for writ remedies, or
whether their remedies must lie within statutory frameworks and appellate mechanisms provided by
law. The judgment could have far-reaching implications for the ED’s legal strategy and for the broader
understanding of writ jurisdiction under the Constitution.

A contract of indemnity basically involves one party promising the other party to make good its losses.
These losses may arise either due to the conduct of the other party or that of somebody else. To
indemnify something basically means to make good a loss. In other words, it means that one party will

called a "contract of indemnity".

XV. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, which has governed contractual relationships in India for over 150
years, underwent a significant transformation with the enactment of the Mediation Act, 2023. This
legislative development resolved a longstanding ambiguity surrounding Section 28 of the Contract Act,
which traditionally rendered void any agreement that absolutely restricted parties from enforcing their
contractual rights through usual legal proceedings.
For decades, multi-tier dispute resolution clauses requiring parties to attempt mediation before
approaching courts or arbitration operated in a legal grey area. Prior to 2023, the only statutory
exception to Section 28 was for arbitration agreements. This created considerable uncertainty for
parties incorporating mandatory pre-litigation mediation clauses in contracts. Various High Courts
adopted divergent approaches, some held that mandatory mediation clauses amounted to absolute
restrictions on access to justice and were void under Section 28, while others took a pragmatic view,
treating such clauses as merely regulating the manner of enforcement.
The Mediation Act, 2023, which received Presidential assent on September 14, 2023, and came into
force through phased implementation starting October 2023, decisively addressed this judicial
inconsistency. Through its Third Schedule, the Act amended Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act by
substituting both Exception 1 and Exception 2 with new provisions that expressly save agreements
referring disputes to mediation from the application of Section 28. The amended exceptions now provide
that agreements referring present or future disputes to either arbitration or mediation shall not
be rendered illegal. www.lawpreptutorial.com
This amendment places mediation on equal statutory footing with arbitration, which has enjoyed such
protection since the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Under Section 27 of the Mediation Act,
mediated settlement agreements are now enforceable as decrees of court in accordance with the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908, granting them status comparable to arbitral awards.
The practical implications have been substantial. Contracts can now legitimately contain mandatory
pre-litigation mediation clauses without fear of being struck down. Courts have begun staying suits and
directing parties to mediation where valid mediation clauses exist. The Act also recognizes online
mediation agreements, encouraging technology-enabled dispute resolution in commercial contracts.
Overall, this legislative reform represents a decisive policy shift towards institutionalized alternative
dispute resolution and provides much-needed clarity to parties seeking efficient mechanisms for conflict
resolution outside traditional litigation.
